assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 60,000 operations/s for ONE city, and the RATIO is the whole lesson: ~96,000 online drivers pinging every 4 seconds = 24,000 position writes/s, plus ~36,000 nearby-driver searches/s from rider apps with the map open, against only ~48 ride requests/s. That is roughly 1,250 location operations for every ride, so a ride-sharing system is a location system with a marketplace attached. CORRECTION: the previous version of this file put ride requests at 1,800/s, which is arithmetically impossible. 1,800/s is 155.5 million rides per day in a single city, against Uber's reported 'more than 40 million trips every day' worldwide (Uber Q4 and full-year 2025 results, 4 Feb 2026) - about 463 trips/s for the entire planet. It was also self-inconsistent: 1,800/s spread over 96,000 drivers is ~67 completed trips per driver per hour. 48/s is ~1.8 trips per driver per hour, which the same fleet can actually deliver. NO PUBLIC FIGURE exists for one city's request rate; 48/s is reasoned from the driver count, not cited. Even 48/s is deliberately the top end - it is ~4.1M trips/day, about a tenth of Uber's entire global volume in one city, which is the largest single-region deployment worth drawing.

assumptions.subject: scope
assumptions.statement: This is a SINGLE-REGION, single-city deployment, which is the v1 scope of the engine. A real ride-sharing platform is sharded per city/region and the interesting failure modes are cross-region ones. Do not read this as a global architecture.

assumptions.subject: loc
assumptions.statement: Location ingest is deliberately a separate, cheap tier from the business API: a ping is a tiny write with no transaction, sized at ~8,000/s per instance. Putting pings through the same app tier as trip requests is the mistake this split exists to prevent. NO PUBLIC per-instance figure exists for Uber's ingest tier, so 8,000/s is reasoned, not cited. It runs 5 instances rather than the minimum 4 because the ping firehose is the one flow that cannot be shed - a driver whose pings stop is invisible to the map and to dispatch - so it is given the largest headroom in the design. That is a stated design choice, not a computed result.

assumptions.subject: nearby_drivers
assumptions.statement: THE READ SIDE OF THE GEO INDEX, which this blueprint previously omitted. Matt Ranney (Uber Chief Systems Architect), QCon London 2015, reported by High Scalability on 14 Sep 2015: the geo index 'design goal is to handle a million writes per second', AND 'the read goal is for many more reads than writes per second because everyone with an open app is doing reads.' The old file had this inverted - 24,000 writes/s against 3,600 reads/s - so the geo tier showed 14% utilisation and read as a write sink with 7x headroom, which is the opposite of the only published statement about the real thing. Modelled here as ~180,000 rider apps open on the map at peak, each redrawing nearby cars every ~5 seconds, giving ~36,000 searches/s against 24,000 writes/s: reads ~1.5x writes. The 180,000 open-app count is an ASSUMPTION - Uber publishes no concurrent-open-app figure for a single city, only Ranney's direction of travel - and it is the number to change first if your city is smaller.

assumptions.subject: geo_write
assumptions.statement: The WRITE half of the geo index: GEOADD (or an H3/S2 cell upsert) on every driver ping. It is a point write at a known key, which is why it is cheap and why ~100,000 ops/s per node is a defensible order of magnitude for Redis. This is the original single `cache` row, kept at its original capacity and latency because no public per-instance figure for Uber's own index exists; the nearest first-party anchor, CacheFront at ~6M RPS over ~3,000 Redis cores (~2,000 RPS/core, 15 Feb 2024), is a different workload and is named here as context, not as this row's source. It runs 2 nodes for failover, not for throughput - at 24,000 writes/s one node would do.

assumptions.subject: geo_search
assumptions.statement: The READ half, split out of the old single `cache` row because the engine charges one flat per-op rate and a radius search is nothing like a point write - charging both at 100,000 ops/s and 0.6 ms is exactly what hid this constraint. Sized at 4,250 queries/s per instance from Uber's Go geofence service: 170k QPS across 40 machines at 35% CPU, p95 under 5 ms and p99 under 50 ms, and 'Uber's highest queries per second (QPS) service out of the hundreds we run in production' (Uber Engineering, 24 Feb 2016). TWO HONESTY NOTES. (a) A geofence lookup answers 'which zone is this point in', a geo-CONFIG read, not a driver radius search - so the anchor is ADJACENT, NOT EXACT. The nearer shape is Uber's orders-near-you radius search on Pinot + H3, published only as 'thousands of queries per second' at P99 50 ms (20 Jul 2021), replacing a Cassandra design that would have needed 'hundreds of thousands' of lookups/s. (b) 4,250 QPS per machine was measured at 35% CPU, so it is an OPERATING POINT, not a measured ceiling; using it as capacity here is deliberately conservative. base_latency_ms 3.0 sits between the geofence p95 and the Pinot P99 and is reasoned, not published.

assumptions.subject: radius_cost
assumptions.statement: A nearby-driver query is an EXPANDING-RADIUS search: it starts at the rider's cell and widens until it has enough candidates, so one user-visible query is more than one index operation. The engine has no spatial cost model, so that cost is expressed as visit_prob above 1 on the search tier - 2 per map refresh, 3 per ride request and 3 per dispatch attempt, because dispatch widens furthest to find any available car. NO PUBLIC FIGURE gives an average probe count; these multipliers are assumptions chosen to represent a dense city. They are the single biggest lever on where this design's bottleneck lands, so a reader modelling a sparser city should lower them before changing anything else.

assumptions.subject: q
assumptions.statement: Only ~25% of pings are persisted to the event log (visit_prob 0.25) — a driver stationary at a light produces no meaningful delta. Persisting every ping would nearly triple the log's write rate and its retention bill.

assumptions.subject: api
assumptions.statement: The API tier now carries the map-refresh polling as well as the money path (trip lifecycle, receipts), which is why it goes from 3 instances to 19. It is provisioned to roughly 63% while the search tier runs at roughly 80%, deliberately: a receipt or a trip-state write must not queue behind ~36,000 map refreshes/s. That is a stated design choice, not a computed result. This tier is also what the push platform below exists to empty - Uber measured that before push, '80% of requests made to the backend API gateway were polling calls' (18 Dec 2020), and that polling is what fills it here.

assumptions.subject: push
assumptions.statement: OUTBOUND TIER, previously missing entirely: every flow in the old file was inbound request/response, which is the exact shape Uber's push platform post says was the problem - before push, '80% of requests made to the backend API gateway were polling calls' (Uber Engineering, 18 Dec 2020). Published scale: RAMEN carried 'over 70,000 QPS push messages per second' over 'up to 600,000 concurrent streaming connections', later 'more than 1.5M concurrent connections and pushes over 250,000 messages per second'; the gRPC successor adds driver offers with 'a validity of 30 seconds' and improved p95 connect latency 'by a minimum of 45%' (16 Aug 2022). Those are FLEET-WIDE figures - Uber publishes no per-instance number - so 8,000 messages/s per instance here is reasoned by analogy with the ping-ingest tier in this same file (both are tiny, transaction-free messages) and is NOT cited. The fan-out share is derived: ~48 trips/s x ~900 s average trip = ~43,000 concurrent trips out of 96,000 online drivers, so ~45% of driver pings are pushed on to a rider watching the car move.

assumptions.subject: match
assumptions.statement: Dispatch is modelled as a per-request service at ~600 matches/s per instance, ~45 ms each. Real dispatch BATCHES requests over a 2-5 second window and solves an assignment problem across all waiting riders and drivers at once, because greedy per-request matching produces worse pairings (Uber's own marketplace page: 'if we wait just a few seconds after a request, it can make a big difference... we evaluate nearby drivers and riders in one batch'). The engine has no batch-window or optimisation model, so this is the closest honest shape, not the real algorithm. Instance count drops from 5 to 1: the 5 were sized against the impossible 1,800 req/s, and at ~48 matches/s one instance is ~8% used. THROUGHPUT IS ALSO THE WRONG WAY TO SIZE THIS SERVICE - real dispatch is a sharded STATEFUL ring with per-entity serialization, not interchangeable stateless replicas (Ranney 2015: 'they are building a stateful service so stateless approaches to scaling won't work'; Uber's Ringpop does the application-level sharding, 4 Feb 2016; the pre-Spanner fulfilment stack managed 'only 20 online drivers/couriers per core', 29 Sep 2021). Process count there is set by owned entities, not by request rate. The engine cannot model that, so 1 instance is the honest reading of THIS model and a real deployment would run many more. It also leaves dispatch a single point of failure here, which is a limit of the model, not a recommendation.

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: The Postgres primary is LEFT UNCHANGED at 12,000 rps on one instance, which at ~288 writes/s is about 2% utilised. That is not a sizing recommendation - it is the honest consequence of fixing the request rate. The old design's 1,800 req/s made the trip store look like it mattered; it does not, and a reader who optimises it is optimising the wrong component. It is left at this class rather than shrunk because no public figure exists for a real trip store's per-instance capacity, and inventing a smaller one would be a different kind of wrong. Size your own store from your own write rate. It remains this design's single point of failure.

assumptions.subject: boundary
assumptions.statement: Maps, routing/ETA and the payment processor are OUTSIDE this model. Keystone has no per-instance price for a third-party API, so including one would mean inventing its cost. Their latency lands on the rider's experience and their rate limits can bind before anything modelled here does.

assumptions.subject: surge
assumptions.statement: Surge pricing, driver incentives, fraud checks and ETA prediction are not modelled. The one that matters for capacity is surge: it is a feedback loop that changes the arrival rate itself, and this is an open queueing network with a fixed offered load.

assumptions.subject: push_concurrency
assumptions.statement: NOT MODELLED, and the reader needs to know: the push tier above is charged per MESSAGE, but a streaming platform's real constraint is CONCURRENT CONNECTIONS and the memory/file descriptors they hold - Uber quotes 1.5M concurrent connections alongside 250,000 messages/s, and this engine has no concurrency dimension at all. Connection churn on a mobile network, reconnect storms after a deploy, and the 30-second validity window on a driver offer are all outside the model. Do not read the push row's utilisation as a capacity plan.

_library.summary: A driver-location firehose plus a heavier nearby-driver read path, with dispatch matching riders to nearby cars and a push tier streaming the result back.
